01.note: Two partners owned a slave together, and one of them freed his half. The other partner worried that the local rabbis would hear of it and make him lose the slave, so he transferred his half to his young son, whom the court could not force to free anyone. Rav Yosef, son of Rava, sent the case to Rav Pappa, who answered with a verse: as he has done, so shall it be done to him. Rav Pappa's plan: since a child is drawn to money, appoint a steward for the boy, have the slave jingle coins in front of him, and write a bill of emancipation in the boy's name.
01.why: The Gemara has just ruled, with Ravina, that a bill of manumission can still be written for slaves whose ownership seemed lost; this case shows the Sages finding a way to free a half-freed slave whose owner tried to block it.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rava
people.about: Sent the case of the half-freed slave to Rav Pappa for a ruling.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Answered that the master's trick should be turned back on him, and laid out how to free the slave.

terms.meaning: A written document by which a master frees a slave. Also called a bill of manumission.
A guardian appointed to manage the property of a child or orphan who cannot legally manage it himself.

02.note: Rabbi Yitzhak reported an incident: a woman who was half slave and half free, whose master was forced to free her completely. The Gemara asks whether this follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka, who held that the blessing 'be fruitful and multiply' was spoken to both Adam and Eve, so a woman too must be able to have children. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak said no: the reason was that men were taking liberties with her, since she could not marry.
02.why: The Gemara has been debating what happens to the betrothal of a woman who is half slave and half free when she is freed; this incident shows a court forcing her full freedom, and the Gemara asks on what grounds.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: Reported the incident, through Rav Huna bar Ketina.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: Sage who held that the command to have children applies to women as well as men.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: Explained that the master was forced to free her because men were taking liberties with her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two partners, one of whom freed his share. She is partly a slave and partly free, and so cannot legally marry either a free Jew or a slave.

03.note: A slave fled from his master outside the Land of Israel into the Land of Israel. His master followed him and came before Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Ami told the master: we will write you a promissory note for the slave's value, and you write him a bill of manumission. If you refuse, I will take him from you altogether, on the authority of Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya. The text does not say what the master did.
03.why: The Gemara has just discussed why a Jew who buys a slave abroad loses him; this case turns to a slave who flees into the Land of Israel, and the discussion after it explains the verse reading of Rabbi Ahai that Rabbi Ami relied on.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage before whom the master came; he pressed the master to free the slave.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Sage whose teaching Rabbi Ami cited as grounds for taking the slave from his master.

terms.meaning: A written document by which a master frees a slave.
A written promise to pay a debt, here for the slave's value, so the master would still be paid.

04.note: Rav Hisda's slave ran away to Bei Kutai, a place where Samaritans lived, and Rav Hisda sent asking them to return him. They answered with the verse 'You shall not deliver to his master a slave.' He replied with the verse on lost property: so you shall do with anything your brother has lost. They sent the first verse back again. Rav Hisda answered that it speaks of a slave who fled from outside the Land of Israel into it, as Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, taught. The text does not say whether the slave was returned.
04.why: The Gemara has been collecting rival readings of the verse about not returning a runaway slave; right after, it asks why Rav Hisda chose Rabbi Ahai's reading and answers that this was how the Samaritans themselves understood the verse.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The master whose slave ran away; he argued by letter with the Samaritans for his return.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Sage whose reading of the verse Rav Hisda cited.

terms.meaning: A place where Samaritans lived. Samaritans were a group who accepted the Torah but not the teachings of the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

05.note: Abaye lost a donkey among the Samaritans of Bei Kutai and sent asking them to send it to him. They asked him to send a distinguishing mark first. He wrote that its belly was white. They sent back that if he were not Nahmani, they would not have sent it, since all donkeys have white bellies.
05.why: It comes right after Rav Hisda's exchange with the same Samaritans of Bei Kutai over his runaway slave, which turned on the verse about returning a brother's lost property.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who lost his donkey; the Samaritans call him Nahmani and trust him.

terms.meaning: A detail that identifies a lost item, which the owner gives to prove it is his before the finder returns it.
A place where Samaritans lived. Samaritans were a group who accepted the Torah but not the teachings of the Sages.

06.note: Rav Nahman's daughters would stir a boiling pot with their bare hands. Rav Ilish puzzled over the verse 'a woman among all these I have not found': what about Rav Nahman's daughters? His words brought on their captivity, and he was taken captive with them. In captivity a man who knew the language of birds told him a raven was calling 'Ilish, escape'; Ilish called the raven a liar. Then a dove said the same, and since Israel is compared to a dove, he took it as a sign of a miracle. He eavesdropped on the daughters and heard them say their captors were now their husbands and they did not want to be redeemed. He fled; he crossed the river by ferry, but the captors caught the other man and killed him. When the daughters came back, Ilish said they had stirred the pot by witchcraft.
06.why: The mishna has just ruled that one may not help captives escape, and the Gemara asked whether that holds when there is only one captive; this tale of an escape from captivity follows.

people.name: Rav Ilish
people.about: Questioned the daughters' righteousness, was taken captive with them, and escaped.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Father of the daughters who stirred the boiling pot and were taken captive.

people.name: the man who knew the language of birds
people.about: A fellow captive who interpreted the birds for Rav Ilish; he fled with him and was killed.

terms.meaning: The Jewish people as a whole, often pictured in the Sages' teachings as a dove.
A town in Babylonia, home of the daughters' husbands.

07.note: An Arab merchant woman brought a sack of phylacteries to Abaye. He asked whether she would give him each pair for a date. She became furious, took the phylacteries and threw them into the river. Abaye said: I should not have belittled them so much in front of her.
07.why: The Sages have just taught that one may pay a gentile somewhat more than their value for sacred objects, up to a small coin; Abaye's lowball offer shows what is lost by paying too little.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who offered a date for each pair of phylacteries and regretted it.

people.name: a certain Arab merchant woman
people.about: Brought the phylacteries to sell, and threw them into the river when insulted by the price.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding handwritten Torah verses, worn by Jewish men during prayer.

08.note: Some residents of Bei Mikhsi borrowed money from gentiles and could not pay it back, so the gentiles came and seized them as slaves. They came before Rav Huna to ask that they be redeemed. Rav Huna said: what can I do for you? We learned that one who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed. Rabbi Abba objected that their teacher had taught that this applies only to one who sold himself three times. Rav Huna answered that these people do this habitually.
08.why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, and Rav Asi limits it to one who did so three times; this case tests that limit against people who fell into debt again and again.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Sage before whom the seized debtors came; he declined to have them redeemed.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Objected to Rav Huna, citing the teaching that the rule applies only after a third sale.

terms.meaning: Bought back out of captivity or slavery, usually with community funds.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

09.note: A man who had sold himself to gladiators came before Rabbi Ami and begged him to redeem him. Rabbi Ami said that if even a self-sold man's children are redeemed to keep them from ruin, all the more so here, where his life is at stake. The Sages told Rabbi Ami the man was an apostate: he had been seen eating meat from carcasses and torn animals. Rabbi Ami said perhaps he ate it out of appetite. They replied that at times he passed over permitted food to eat forbidden food. So Rabbi Ami told the man: Go, they do not allow me to redeem you.
09.why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, though his children are; Rabbi Ami argues that the danger of death should outweigh that rule, until the man's open rejection of Jewish law decides it.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who wanted to redeem the man but was stopped by the Sages.

terms.meaning: Men who fought to the death for public entertainment; selling oneself to them put one's life at risk.
A Jew who has deliberately rejected Jewish law.
Meat forbidden to Jews: from animals that died without proper slaughter, or from animals with a fatal injury or defect.

10.note: Reish Lakish sold himself to gladiators and took with him a bag with a round stone inside. He knew that on a captive's last day his captors grant whatever he asks. On his last day they asked what he wanted. He said he wished to tie them up, seat them, and strike each one a blow and a half. He tied them and seated them, and each one he struck once died. Gritting his teeth, he said to each dead man: are you laughing at me? You still have half a blow coming. He killed them all. He came home and sat eating and drinking. When his daughter asked if he wanted something to lie on, he said: my belly is my pillow. When he died he left only a kav of saffron, and recited of himself the verse 'they leave their wealth to others'.
10.why: It follows the case of an apostate who sold himself to gladiators and could not be redeemed; here a great Sage who sold himself to gladiators frees himself.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: Sage who sold himself to gladiators and killed them on his last day; known here for his great strength.

people.name: his daughter
people.about: Asked Reish Lakish whether he wanted something to lie on.

terms.meaning: Men who fought to the death for public entertainment.
A small measure of volume, a few pints.

11.note: A steward for orphans in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood was selling the orphans' land and buying slaves, and Rabbi Meir would not let him. In a dream Rabbi Meir was shown the words: I wish to destroy and you build? Even so, he paid no attention, saying that words in dreams neither raise nor lower anything.
11.why: The teaching just quoted forbids stewards to sell orphans' fields to buy slaves, since land is the safer asset; this case shows Rabbi Meir enforcing that rule even against a dream.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage who stopped the steward and ignored a dream that seemed to tell him otherwise.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.

12.note: Two men, incited by Satan, quarreled with each other every Friday at twilight. Rabbi Meir came to their place and held them back three Friday evenings in a row until he made peace between them. Then he heard Satan say: Woe, Rabbi Meir has driven that man out of his house.
12.why: The Gemara says it tells this one because it has just told another story about Rabbi Meir and a steward for orphans.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage who made peace between the two quarreling men.

people.name: Satan
people.about: Incited the quarrel, and lamented when Rabbi Meir ended it.

terms.meaning: The hour just before the Sabbath begins, when tension is high as preparations must be finished.

13.note: A steward for orphans in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's neighborhood was selling the orphans' land and buying oxen, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said nothing to him at all.
13.why: The rule just taught forbids selling orphans' land to buy slaves; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi agreed with Rabbi Yosei, who called his ox 'my field', so oxen count as land.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage who saw the steward trade land for oxen and did not object.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who said he never called his wife 'my wife' but 'my home', nor his ox 'my ox' but 'my field'.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.

14.note: Some orphans lived with an old woman, and they owned an ox, which she took and sold for them. Their relatives came before Rav Nahman asking what right she had to sell. He said the mishna speaks of orphans who live with a householder, so she counts as their steward. They objected that the ox had since gone up in value; he said it rose while in the buyer's hands. They objected that the orphans had not yet been paid. Rav Nahman said that in that case Shmuel's rule applies: orphans' property is like consecrated property and changes hands only when money is paid. The text does not say how the sale ended.
14.why: It follows a run of cases about stewards of orphans' property; this one asks who may act as steward without being appointed, and leads into Shmuel's rule on when an orphans' sale becomes final.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage before whom the orphans' relatives challenged the sale.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose rule on orphans' property Rav Nahman cited.

people.name: Rav Hanilai bar Idi
people.about: Passed on Shmuel's rule about orphans' property.

terms.meaning: Property given to the Temple. By law it changes hands only when money is paid, not by the buyer taking hold of it as with ordinary goods.
A guardian who manages orphans' property for them.

15.note: Buyers took possession of the wine of Rabbana Ukva, an orphan, at four dinars a barrel. Before they paid, its price rose to six. The parties came before Rav Nahman, who said this case falls under Shmuel's rule: orphans' property is like consecrated property and changes hands only when money is paid.
15.why: It applies the rule Rav Nahman cited in the case just before; the Gemara then works out when that rule helps orphans, and Rav Sheisha objects that it could harm them.

people.name: Rabbana Ukva
people.about: An orphan whose wine rose in price before the buyers had paid.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who ruled on the sale of the wine.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage whose rule on orphans' property Rav Nahman cited.

terms.meaning: A legal act of acquisition: taking physical hold of goods. For ordinary goods this finalizes a purchase.
Property given to the Temple, which changes hands only when money is paid.

16.note: Amram the dyer was a steward for orphans. The orphans' relatives came to Rav Nahman and said he dressed himself in fine clothes from the orphans' property. Rav Nahman said: perhaps so that his words will be listened to. They said he ate and drank from their property though he was not known to be rich. Rav Nahman said: say he found something valuable. They said he was causing them losses. Rav Nahman said: bring me witnesses that he causes losses and I will remove him, citing Rav Huna in Rav's name that a steward who causes losses is removed.
16.why: The Gemara is working through the duties of a steward for orphans; this case sets the rule, disputed by the school of Rabbi Sheila, that a steward who causes loss is removed, and the Gemara rules that he is.

people.name: Amram the dyer
people.about: Steward for orphans, accused by their relatives of living off their property.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Sage who heard the complaints and asked for witnesses before removing the steward.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reported in Rav's name that a steward who causes losses is removed.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed to manage the property of orphans until they are old enough to manage it themselves.
The binding ruling in Jewish law.

17.note: One man insulted another, calling him a convert, son of a convert. The second man shot back: at least I don't eat produce of the Sabbatical Year the way you do.
17.why: The Gemara is explaining why Rabbi Yehuda imposed no penalty for unknowingly breaking the Sabbatical Year rules: in his place it was treated as very serious, and this exchange, where eating its produce is the worse insult, is the proof.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when fields in the Land of Israel must lie fallow and their produce may not be traded or treated as ordinary.
Someone who became Jewish rather than being born Jewish; here the word is used as an insult.

18.note: A man told another: the ritually pure food I prepared with you on such and such a day became impure. The owner came before Rabbi Ami, who said that in principle the man is not believed. Rabbi Asi said to him: My teacher, do you say this? Rabbi Yohanan said in Rabbi Yosei's name: What can I do, when the Torah believed him? The text does not say how Rabbi Ami responded.
18.why: A teaching just quoted says a helper is believed that food became impure while he is still working on it, but not about a past day; Rabbi Asi's report challenges that, and the Gemara next asks where the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who ruled that the man is not believed about the past.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Challenged Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Reported Rabbi Yosei's saying that the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who said, What can I do, when the Torah believed him?

terms.meaning: Food kept free of ritual impurity, a religious status that contact with certain things can transfer. Impure food could not be eaten by those keeping these rules.

19.note: A scribe came before Rabbi Ami and said that in the Torah scroll he wrote for a client, he had not written God's names with the proper intention. Rabbi Ami asked who had the scroll; the buyer did. Rabbi Ami said: you are believed to lose your wage, but not to make the Torah scroll unfit. Rabbi Yirmeya asked: granted he loses his wage for the names, does he lose his wage for the whole scroll? Rabbi Ami said yes, since a Torah scroll whose names of God were not written with proper intention is worth nothing.
19.why: The Gemara is asking when a person is believed about past work he did for others; next it asks why the scribe was not told to go over the names again, and whose opinion that follows.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who ruled that the scribe's confession costs him his wage but does not disqualify the scroll.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Asked whether the scribe loses his pay for the whole scroll.

terms.meaning: A scribe must consciously intend each name of God as holy as he writes it; without that, the name, and so the scroll, is invalid.

20.note: A scribe came before Rabbi Abbahu and said that he had not prepared the parchment of a Torah scroll he wrote for a client with the proper intention. Rabbi Abbahu asked who had the scroll; the buyer did. Rabbi Abbahu said: since you are believed to lose your wage, you are believed to make the Torah scroll unfit.
20.why: It contrasts with Rabbi Ami's ruling just before; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami's scribe may have lied, thinking he would lose only part of his pay, while this scribe knew he was giving up his entire wage, so he is believed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sage who ruled that the scribe's confession disqualifies the scroll.

terms.meaning: Animal skin prepared for writing. For a Torah scroll it must be processed with the intention that it is for that holy use.
